{{official URL}} | country = United States }} The '''Congressional Progressive Caucus''' ('''CPC''') is a [[congressional caucus]] affiliated with the [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic Party]] in the [[United States Congress]].{{cite web|url=https://cpc-grijalva.house.gov/caucus-members/|title=Congressional Progressive Caucus: Caucus Members|work=house.gov}} The CPC represents the most [[Left-wing politics|left-leaning]] faction of the Democratic Party.{{cite book|publisher=Beacon Press|isbn=978-0807043172|title=Mobilizing Resentment: Conservative Resurgence From The John Birch Society To The Promise Keepers|url=https://archive.org/details/mobilizingresent00hard|url-access=registration|last=Hardisty|first=Jean|location=Boston|year=2000|page=[https://archive.org/details/mobilizingresent00hard/page/221 221]}}{{cite web|title=Two congressmen endorse Carl Sciortino in race to replace Markey in Congress|url=http://www.boston.com/yourtown/news/medford/2013/09/two_congressmen_endorse_carl_sciortino_in_race_to_replace_ma.html|publisher=[[Boston.com]]|access-date=July 23, 2014|date=September 13, 2013}} "[T]he Congressional Progressive Caucus, the umbrella group for left-leaning Democratic members of Congress". It was founded in 1991 and has grown since then. As of March 22, 2022, of the [[117th United States Congress]], the CPC has 101 members (99 voting [[United States House of Representatives|Representatives]], 1 non-voting Delegate, and 1 [[United States Senate|Senator]]), making it the largest ideological caucus in the Democratic Party (slightly larger than the [[New Democrat Coalition]]) and the second largest ideological caucus overall (after the [[Republican Study Committee]]). The CPC is chaired by U.S. Representative [[Pramila Jayapal]] (D-WA). == History == The CPC was established in 1991 by U.S. Representatives [[Ron Dellums]] (D-CA), [[Lane Evans]] (D-IL), [[Thomas Andrews (American politician)|Thomas Andrews]] (D-ME), [[Peter DeFazio]] (D-OR), [[Maxine Waters]] (D-CA) and [[Bernie Sanders]] (I-VT). Additional Representatives joined soon thereafter, including [[Major Owens]] (D-NY), [[Nydia Velázquez]] (D-NY), [[David Bonior]] (D-MI), [[Bob Filner]] (D-CA), [[Barney Frank]] (D-MA), [[Maurice Hinchey]] (D-NY), [[Jim McDermott]] (D-WA), [[Jerry Nadler]] (D-NY), [[Patsy Mink]] (D-HI), [[George Miller (California politician)|George Miller]] (D-CA), [[Pete Stark]] (D-CA), [[John Olver]] (D-MA) and [[Lynn Woolsey]] (D-CA). Sanders was the first CPC Chairman.{{cite magazine |last1=Talbot |first1=Margaret |title=The Populist Prophet |url=https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2015/10/12/the-populist-prophet |magazine=The New Yorker |date=October 5, 2015 |access-date=19 May 2020}} The founding CPC members were concerned about the economic hardship imposed by the deepening recession and the growing inequality brought about by the timidity of the [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic Party]] response in the early 1990s. On January 3, 1995, at a standing room only news conference on Capitol Hill, they were the first group inside Congress to chart a comprehensive legislative alternative to U.S. Speaker Newt Gingrich and the Republican [[Contract with America]]. The CPC's ambitious agenda was framed as "The Progressive Promise: Fairness".{{cite web |last1=Brodey |first1=Sam |title=How Keith Ellison made the Congressional Progressive Caucus into a political force that matters |url=https://www.minnpost.com/dc-dispatches/2015/07/how-keith-ellison-made-congressional-progressive-caucus-political-force-matter/ |website=MinnPost |date=July 21, 2015 |access-date=19 May 2020}} === List of chairs === [[File:Pramila Jayapal, official portrait, 116th Congress.jpg|thumb|160px|right|Chairwoman [[Pramila Jayapal]], from [[Washington's 7th congressional district]]]] {|class="wikitable" !Term start !Term end !colspan=2|Chair(s) |- |1991 |1999 |colspan=2 |

|} == Policy positions == {{social democracy sidebar}} {{modern liberalism in the United States sidebar}} The CPC advocates "a universal, high-quality, [[Medicare for All]] health care system for all", [[living wage]] laws, reductions in military expenditure, a crackdown on corporate greed, putting an end to [[Incarceration in the United States|mass incarceration]], supporting and implementing swift measures to start reversing climate change, immigration policies that are humane, and [[reparations for slavery|reparations]].{{cite web|publisher=Congressional Progressive Caucus|title=The Progressive Promise|access-date=December 18, 2020|url=https://cpc-grijalva.house.gov/the-progressive-promise/}} ===Economy=== In April 2011, the CPC released a proposed "People's Budget" for fiscal year 2012.{{cite web|title=The People's Budget|url=http://grijalva.house.gov/uploads/The%20CPC%20FY2012%20Budget.pdf|access-date=April 24, 2011|publisher=Congressional Progressive Caucus}} Two of its proponents stated: "By implementing a fair tax code, by building a resilient American economy, and by bringing our troops home, we achieve a budget surplus of over $30 billion by 2021 and we end up with a debt that is less than 65% of our GDP. This is what sustainability looks like".{{citation|last1=Honda|first1=Michael|title=The only real Democratic budget|date=April 11, 2011|url=http://thehill.com/blogs/congress-blog/economy-a-budget/155221-the-only-real-democratic-budget|newspaper=[[The Hill (newspaper)|The Hill]]|access-date=March 24, 2018|last2=Grijalva|first2=Raul|author-link=Michael Honda|author2-link=Raul Grijalva}} In 2019, the [[Party divisions of United States Congresses|Democratic-controlled]] [[United States House of Representatives|House of Representatives]] passed H.R.582, ''The Raise the Wage Act'',https://www.congress.gov/bill/116th-congress/house-bill/582#:~:text=Passed%20House%20(07%2F18%2F2019)&text=(Sec.,less%20than%2020%20years%20old. which would have gradually raised the minimum wage to $15 per hour. It was not taken up in the Republican-controlled [[United States Senate|Senate]]. In January 2021, Democrats in the Senate and House of Representatives reintroduced the bill.[https://www.cnbc.com/2019/01/16/house-democrats-introduce-bill-to-hike-minimum-wage-to-15-per-hour.html "Democrats introduce bill to hike federal minimum wage to $15 per hour"], ''[[CNBC]]'', January 16, 2019. In February 2021, the [[Congressional Budget Office]] released a report on the Raise the Wage Act of 2021 which estimated that incrementally raising the federal minimum wage to $15 an hour by 2025 would benefit 17 million workers, but would also reduce employment by 1.4 million people.{{ cite web | url=https://www.cbo.gov/system/files/2021-02/56975-Minimum-Wage.pdf | title=The Budgetary Effects of the Raise the Wage Act of 2021 | last= | first= | work=[[Congressional Budget Office]] | date=February 1, 2021 | access-date=February 9, 2021 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210208225338/https://www.cbo.gov/system/files/2021-02/56975-Minimum-Wage.pdf | archive-date=February 8, 2021 | url-status=live }}{{ cite news | url=https://www.npr.org/2021/02/08/965483266/-15-minimum-wage-would-reduce-poverty-but-cost-jobs-cbo-says | title=$15 Minimum Wage Would Reduce Poverty But Cost Jobs, CBO Says | last=Selyukh | first=Alina | newspaper=[[NPR]] | date=February 8, 2021 | quote=Raising the federal minimum wage to $15 an hour by 2025 would increase wages for at least 17 million people, but also put 1.4 million Americans out of work, according to a study by the Congressional Budget Office released on Monday. }}{{Cite news |last=Rosenberg |first=Eli |date=February 8, 2021 |title=CBO report finds $15 minimum wage would cost jobs but lower poverty levels |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/business/2021/02/08/minimum-wage-hike-15-an-hour-by-2025-would-result-14-million-unemployed-nonpartisan-congressional-budget-office-says/ |newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] |quote=Raising the minimum wage to $15 an hour would significantly reduce poverty and increase earnings for millions of low-wage workers, while adding to the federal deficit and cutting overall employment, according to a new study from the nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office. ... On one hand, the CBO estimated that raising the minimum wage to $15 an hour by 2025 would cost 1.4 million jobs and increase the deficit by $54 billion over 10 years. But it also estimated the policy would lift 900,000 people out of poverty and raise income for 17 million people — about 1 in 10 workers. Another 10 million who have wages just above that amount could potentially see increases, as well, the CBO reported.}} On February 27, 2021, the Democratic-controlled House passed the [[American Rescue Plan Act of 2021|American Rescue Plan]] [[COVID-19 pandemic|pandemic]] relief package, which included a gradual minimum wage increase to $15 per hour.[https://www.washingtonpost.com/us-policy/2021/02/26/american-rescue-plan-house-coronavirus-stimulus/ "American Rescue Plan: What's in the House's $1.9 trillion coronavirus relief plan"], ''[[Washington Post]]'', February 27, 2021. The measure was ultimately removed from the Senate version of the bill.[https://www.washingtonpost.com/us-policy/2021/03/06/biden-stimulus-covid-relief "Senate passes $1.9 trillion Biden relief bill after voting overnight on amendments, sends measure back to House"], ''[[Washington Post]]'', March 6, 2021. ===Climate change=== [[File:GreenNewDeal Presser 020719 (26 of 85) (46105848855).jpg|thumb|250px|Representative [[Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez]] speaks on the [[Green New Deal]] with Senator [[Ed Markey]] in front of the Capitol Building in February 2019.]] A prominent 2019 attempt to get legislation passed for a Green New Deal was sponsored by Rep. [[Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez]] (D-NY) and Sen. [[Ed Markey]] (D-MA) during the [[116th United States Congress]], though it failed to advance in the Senate.{{cite news |last1=Rebecca Shabad |last2=Dartunorro Clark |title=Senate fails to advance Green New Deal as Democrats protest McConnell 'sham vote' |url=https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/congress/senate-fails-advance-green-new-deal-democrats-protest-mcconnell-sham-n987506 |access-date=April 4, 2019 |work=NBC News |date=March 26, 2019 |archive-date=July 15, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190715013853/https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/congress/senate-fails-advance-green-new-deal-democrats-protest-mcconnell-sham-n987506 |url-status=live }} [[Green New Deal]] proposals call for [[public policy]] to address [[climate change]] along with achieving other social aims like job creation and reducing [[economic inequality]]. The name refers back to the [[New Deal]], a set of [[social reform|social]] and [[economic reform]]s and [[public works project]]s undertaken by President [[Franklin D. Roosevelt]] in response to the [[Great Depression]].Jeremy Lovell (July 21, 2008) [https://www.reuters.com/article/environmentNews/idUSL204610020080721 "Climate report calls for green 'New Deal'"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200610233547/https://www.reuters.com/article/us-climate-deal/climate-report-calls-for-green-new-deal-idUSL204610020080721 |date=June 10, 2020 }}, Reuters. The Green New Deal combines Roosevelt's economic approach with modern ideas such as [[renewable energy]] and [[resource efficiency]].[https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3347494 A Green New Deal: Discursive Review and Appraisal.] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210224075104/https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3347494 |date=February 24, 2021 }} ''Macroeconomics: Aggregative Models eJournal.'' Social Science Research Network (SSRN). Accessed March 14, 2019.[https://www.boell.de/en/2013/11/25/toward-transatlantic-green-new-deal Hilary French, Michael Renner and Gary Gardner: Toward a Transatlantic Green New Deal] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140329163548/http://www.boell.de/en/2013/11/25/toward-transatlantic-green-new-deal |date=March 29, 2014 }} The authors state: "Support is growing around the world for an integrated response to the current economic and environmental crises, increasingly referred to as the "Green New Deal". The term is a modern-day variation of the U.S. New Deal, an ambitious effort launched by President Franklin Roosevelt to lift the United States out of the Great Depression. The New Deal of that era entailed a strong government role in economic planning and a series of stimulus packages launched between 1933 and 1938 that created jobs through ambitious governmental programs, including the construction of roads, trails, dams, and schools. Today's Green New Deal proposals are also premised on the importance of decisive governmental action, but incorporate policies to respond to pressing environmental challenges through a new paradigm of sustainable economic progress." ===Health care=== The [[United States National Health Care Act]], also known as Medicare for All or Expanded and Improved Medicare for All Act, is a bill first introduced in the [[United States House of Representatives]] by Representative [[John Conyers]] (D-MI) in 2003, with 38 co-sponsors.{{USBill|108|HR|676}}[http://www.beckershospitalreview.com/racs-/-icd-9-/-icd-10/house-reps-introduce-medicare-for-all-bill.html "House Reps Introduce Medicare-for-All Bill"] ''Becker's Hospital Review'', Feb. 14, 2013 In 2019, the original 16-year-old proposal was renumbered, and [[Pramila Jayapal]] (D-WA) introduced a broadly similar, but more detailed, bill,{{Cite web|date=2019-02-02|title=Medicare for All bill loses its special number|url=https://www.modernhealthcare.com/article/20190202/NEWS/190139976/medicare-for-all-bill-loses-its-special-number|access-date=2019-06-17|website=Modern Healthcare|language=en}} HR 1384, in the [[116th United States Congress|116th Congress]].{{Cite web|date=2019-02-27|title=Dingell, Jayapal and more than 100 Co-Sponsors Introduce Medicare For All Act of 2019|url=https://debbiedingell.house.gov/news/documentsingle.aspx?DocumentID=1659|access-date=2019-06-18|website=U.S. Representative Debbie Dingell|language=en}} {{As of|2019|November|3|df=US}}, it had 116 co-sponsors still in the House at the time, or 49.8% of House Democrats.{{cite web|title=H.R.1384 – Medicare for All Act of 2019|url=https://www.congress.gov/bill/116th-congress/house-bill/1384/all-info#cosponsors-content|access-date=2019-11-03|publisher=U.S. Congress}} The act would establish a universal [[single-payer health care]] system in the United States, the rough equivalent of [[Medicare (Canada)|Canada's Medicare]] and [[Republic of China|Taiwan]]'s [[Healthcare in Taiwan|Bureau of National Health Insurance]], among other examples. Under a single-payer system, most medical care would be paid for by the [[Government of the United States|federal government]], ending the need for private health insurance and premiums, and re-casting private insurance companies as providing purely supplemental coverage, to be used when non-essential care is sought. The national system would be paid for in part through taxes replacing insurance premiums, but also by savings realized through the provision of preventive universal health care and the elimination of insurance company [[Overhead (business)|overhead]] and hospital billing costs.{{cite news|last=Krugman |first=Paul |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2005/06/13/opinion/13krugman.html |title=One Nation, Uninsured |work=The New York Times |date=June 13, 2005 |access-date=December 4, 2011}}On September 13, 2017, Senator [[Bernie Sanders]] (I-VT) introduced a parallel bill in the [[United States Senate]], with 16 co-sponsors.{{Cite web |url=http://www.newsweek.com/bernie-sanders-sponsor-single-payer-healthcare-bill-574403|title=Bernie Sanders to Sponsor Single-Payer Healthcare Bill |website=Newsweek |date=Mar 26, 2017}}{{cite tweet |author=RoseAnn DeMoro |user=RoseAnnDeMoro |number=908031640995168256 |date=September 13, 2017 |title=.@BernieSanders shouts out the Democrats that did the right thing in supporting #MedicareForAll. #WednesdayWisdom |access-date=13 September 2017}}{{Cite web|url=https://www.congress.gov/bill/115th-congress/house-bill/676|title=115th United States Congress |date=2017–2018 |publisher=U.S. Congress }} The act would establish a universal single-payer health care system in the United States. ====Drug costs==== In 2019, the CPC challenged House Speaker [[Nancy Pelosi]] regarding the details of a drug-pricing bill, the [[Elijah Cummings Lower Drug Costs Now Act]].{{Cite web|last1=Dayen|first1=David|last2=Grimm|first2=Ryan|date=December 9, 2019|title=House Progressives Challenge Nancy Pelosi on Drug-Pricing Bill|url=https://theintercept.com/2019/12/09/bernie-sanders-elizabeth-warren-progressives-drug-pricing-bill/|access-date=2021-01-04|website=The Intercept|language=en}} The final version was the result of extensive negotiations between House Democratic leadership and members of the CPC.{{Cite web|last=Zhou|first=Li|date=2019-12-12|title=The House just passed an ambitious bill to lower prescription drug prices|url=https://www.vox.com/2019/12/12/21010905/house-democrats-pass-prescription-drug-price-bill|access-date=2021-01-04|website=Vox|language=en}} The bill was introduced into the [[United States House of Representatives|House of Representatives]] on September 19, 2019 during the [[116th United States Congress|116th Congress]] by [[Frank Pallone|Rep. Frank Pallone]] ([[Democratic Party (United States)|D]]-[[New Jersey|NJ]]). The bill received 106 co-sponsors.{{Cite web|last=Pallone|first=Frank|date=2020-09-08|title=Cosponsors – H.R.3 – 116th Congress (2019–2020): Elijah E. Cummings Lower Drug Costs Now Act|url=https://www.congress.gov/bill/116th-congress/house-bill/3/cosponsors|access-date=2021-04-07|website=www.congress.gov|archive-date=2021-04-13|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210413021450/https://www.congress.gov/bill/116th-congress/house-bill/3/cosponsors|url-status=live}} It passed the House on December 12, 2019, by a vote of ([https://projects.propublica.org/represent/votes/116/house/1/682 230-192]). All Democrats voted for the measure, and all but 2 Republicans voted against it. The bill was then sent to the [[United States Senate|Senate]]. The Senate, having been controlled by [[Republican Party (United States)|Republicans]], did not bring the bill up for a vote. ====Abortion rights==== During the [[117th United States Congress]] congresswoman [[Judy Chu]] (CA-27) introduced the [[Women's Health Protection Act]]. The act would expand abortion rights and codify [[Roe v. Wade]]. It was introduced in response to the [[Texas Heartbeat Act]]. It passed [[United States House of Representatives|House of Representatives]] (218–211), but was defeated in the [[United States Senate|Senate]] on a 46–48 vote in February 2022.{{Cite web|last=Chu|first=Judy|date=2021-09-21|title=H.R.3755 - 117th Congress (2021-2022): Women's Health Protection Act of 2021|url=https://www.congress.gov/bill/117th-congress/house-bill/3755|access-date=2021-09-24|website=Congress.gov}}{{cite news |last1=Kapur |first1=Sahil |last2=Vitali |first2=Ali |title=Senate rejects Democratic bill to codify abortion rights |url=https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/congress/senate-rejects-democratic-bill-codify-abortion-rights-rcna17968 |access-date=May 3, 2022 |work=NBC News |date=February 28, 2022}} ===2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine=== In October 2022, 30 members of the caucus urged the Biden administration to seek a negotiated, diplomatic end to the [[Russian invasion of Ukraine]] while advocating for continued economic and military support to Ukraine.{{cite news |last1=Schonfeld |first1=Zach |title=Progressives urge Biden to push harder for Ukraine peace talks |url=https://thehill.com/homenews/house/3702113-progressives-urge-biden-to-push-harder-for-ukraine-peace-talks/ |access-date=25 October 2022 |work=The Hill |date=24 October 2022}}{{Cite web |last=Trudo |first=Hanna |date=2022-10-25 |title=Progressive Caucus tries to clarify call for Biden to find diplomatic solution to Ukraine |url=https://thehill.com/homenews/house/3702537-progressive-caucus-tries-to-clarify-call-for-biden-to-find-diplomatic-solution-to-ukraine/ |access-date=2022-10-25 |website=The Hill |language=en-US}} The next day, after a wave of criticism, the letter was swiftly withdrawn on the basis that peaceful negotiations with Putin in current situation are "nearly impossible". Jayapal reasserted the Democrats' support for Ukraine and said the letter had been drafted several months ago and "released by staff without vetting."Wang, Amy B; Abutaleb, Yasmeen; and Sotomayor, Marianna (October 25, 2022) [https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/2022/10/25/democrats-ukraine-letter/ "Liberal Democrats withdraw letter to Biden that urged him to rethink Ukraine strategy"] ''[[The Washington Post]]'' == Electoral results == {| class="wikitable" ! rowspan="2" |Election year ! colspan="4" |Senate ! colspan="3" |House of Representatives |- !
